rows.speaker: علي
rows.claim: Ibn Mardawayh reports the Prophet identifying Ali and his Shi'a as the best creatures, promising their meeting at the Pool when nations gather for judgment.
rows.anchor: أخرج ابن مردويه عن علي كرم الله تعالى وجهه قال قال لي رسول الله صلى الله تعالى عليه وسلم ألم تسمع قول الله تعالى إن الذين آمنوا

rows.speaker: يزيد بن شراحيل الأنصاري
rows.claim: An Imami narration says the Prophet gave Ali this identification at his death, with his head resting on Ali's chest.
rows.anchor: وروي نحوه الإمامية عن يزيد بن شراحيل الأنصاري كاتب الأمير كرم الله تعالى وجهه وفيه أنه عليه الصلاة والسلام قال ذلك له عند الوفاة

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn Mardawayh transmits Ibn Abbas's report that Ali and his Shi'a will be content and approved on Judgment Day.
rows.anchor: وأخرج ابن مردويه أيضا عن ابن عباس قال لما نزلت هذه الآية إن الذين آمنوا الخ قال رسول الله صلى الله تعالى عليه وسلم لعلي رضي الله تعالى عنه

rows.speaker: الطبرسي
rows.claim: Al-Tabarsi cites Muqatil, through al-Dahhak from Ibn Abbas, saying the verse was revealed about Ali and his family; if sound, this means inclusion in its general meaning, not exclusivity.
rows.anchor: ما ذكره الطبرسي الإمامي في مجمع البيان عن مقاتل بن سليمان عن الضحاك عن ابن عباس أنه قال في الآية نزلت في علي كرم الله تعالى وجهه وأهل بيته

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The reports do not make Ali or his Shi'a, nor Ali and his family, the exclusive referent; the earlier claim is unsound because it would imply Ali is better than the Prophet, which even the Imamis deny.
rows.anchor: لا ينبغي أن يرتاب في عدم تخصيص الذين آمنوا وعملوا الصالحات بالأمير كرم الله تعالى وجهه وشيعته

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A report that much of the surah was abrogated gives Ubayy an expanded recitation, but Ibn Mardawayh's version conflicts with what is soundly transmitted from Ubayy and is not relied upon.
rows.anchor: أخرج ذلك ابن مردويه عن أبي رضي الله تعالى عنه وهو مخالف لما صح عنه فلا يعول عليه

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn Abbas, Mujahid, and Ata are cited for a Meccan classification; Qatada and Muqatil are cited for a Medinan classification.
rows.anchor: وهي مكية في قول ابن عباس ومجاهد وعطاء ومدنية في قول قتادة ومقاتل

rows.speaker: أبو سعيد الخدري
rows.claim: A report used to support the Medinan view has Abu Sa'id ask the Prophet whether he would see his deeds; its setting is Medina, and Abu Sa'id reached maturity only after Uhud.
rows.anchor: بما أخرجه ابن أبي حاتم عن أبي سعيد الخدري رضي الله تعالى عنه قال لما نزلت فمن يعمل مثقال

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The surah has eight verses in the Kufan and first Medinan counts, and nine in the other counts.
rows.anchor: وآيها ثمان في الكوفي والمدني الأول وتتسع في الباقية

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: A sound report from Ibn Abbas raises the surah's merit to half the Qur'an; the explanation offered is that it summarizes afterlife rulings and adds the Earth's expulsion of burdens and testimony beyond al-Qari'a.
rows.anchor: وصح في حديث الترمذي والبيهقي وغيرهما عن ابن عباس مرفوعا إذا زلزلت تعدل نصف القرآن

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Another report calls it a quarter because belief in resurrection, which the surah establishes, is one quarter of faith in a four-part hadith.
rows.anchor: وما في الآخر بأن الإيمان بالبعث الذي قررته هذه السورة ربع الإيمان

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The previous surah's account of the two groups' recompense prompts the question of when it will occur, which this surah answers.
rows.anchor: لما ذكر عز وجل في السورة السابقة جزاء الفريقين المؤمنين والكافرين كان ذلك كالمحرك للسؤال عن وقته

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Earth undergoes a violent, repeated earthquake: either its uniquely appointed, unsurpassed quake or its immeasurably wondrous quake; the definite annexation can signal a known quake or, rhetorically, all its quaking.
rows.anchor: حركت تحريكا عنيفا متداركا متكررا زلزالها أي الزلزال المخصوص بها الذي تقتضيه بحسب المشيئة الإلهية

rows.speaker: الجحدري
rows.claim: Al-Jahdari and Isa read zalzalaha with a fatḥa on the first z; Ibn Atiyya treats it as a verbal noun like the kasra form, while al-Zamakhshari calls it a name for the known motion used here in place of the verbal noun.
rows.anchor: وقرأ الجحدري وعيسى زلزالها بفتح الزاي وهو عند ابن عطية مصدر كالزلزال بالكسر وقال الزمخشري

rows.speaker: الزمخشري
rows.claim: Al-Zamakhshari says the kasra form is a verbal noun and the fatḥa form a noun for the familiar movement, metaphorically filling the verbal-noun role here.
rows.anchor: المكسور مصدر والمفتوح اسم للحركة المعروفة وانتصب ههنا على المصدر تجوزا لسده مسد المصدر

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A group places this earthquake at the second blast, on the basis of the following verse.
rows.anchor: وهذا الزلزال على ما ذهب إليه جمع عند النفخة الثانية لقوله تعالى

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn Abbas explains the Earth's burdens as its dead; al-Naqqash, al-Zajjaj, and Mundhir ibn Sa'id say treasures and the dead, a view also transmitted from Ibn Abbas.
rows.anchor: فقد قال ابن عباس أي موتاها وقال النقاش والزجاج ومنذر بن سعيد أي كنوزها وموتاها وروي عن ابن عباس أيضا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: On the treasure reading, these are distinct from the treasures released during the Dajjal's time: some may emerge then and the rest at the second blast, with no bar to further treasures remaining afterward.
rows.anchor: وهذه الكنوز على هذا القول غير الكنوز التي تخرج أيام الدجال على ما وردت به الأخبار

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Other accounts place the release at the first blast, interpret the burdens as treasures or both treasures and dead, or let the event span both blasts; one possibility has the dead emerge first and be revived at the second, though this conflicts with the texts.
rows.anchor: وقيل يحتمل أن يكون إخراج الموتى كالكنوز عند النفخة الأولى وإحياؤها في النفخة الثانية

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Another view assigns treasures to the first blast and the dead to the second, treating the quake as covering both times.
rows.anchor: وقيل إنها تزلزل عند النفخة الأولى فتخرج كنوزها وتزلزل عند الثانية فتخرج موتاها

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Some say treasures emerge at Judgment so the sinners regret having disobeyed over wealth that can no longer help them; a hadith depicts murderers, kin-breakers, and thieves identifying the gold and silver they once killed, severed kinship, or lost a hand for, then leaving it untouched.
rows.anchor: تخرج الأرض كنوزها يوم القيامة ليراها أهل الموقف فيتحسر العصاة إذا نظروا إليها حيث عصوا الله تعالى فيها

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A further explanation is that the treasure emerges to brand the hoarders' foreheads, sides, and backs.
rows.anchor: وقيل إن ذلك لتتكون بها جباه الذين كنزوا وجنوبهم وظهورهم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Athqal is the plural of burden/precious stored property and is metaphorical for treasures, or may mean a womb's load by metaphor; al-Murtada likewise allows the latter only metaphorically. Explaining it as secrets is distant and contrary to transmitted usage.
rows.anchor: فالأثقال جمع ثقل بالتحريك وهو على ما في القاموس متاع المسافر وكل نفيس مصون وتجوز به ههنا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Earth is named again for emphasis, to hint at its replacement, or to show that its quake causes the expulsion as shaking a carpet releases dust; the author instead sees no intended cause-and-effect sequence, only events listed together.
rows.anchor: ولعل الظاهر أنه لم ترد السببية والمسببية بل ذكر كل مما ذكر من الحوادث من غير تعرض لتسبب شيء منها على الآخر

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Every human asks in alarm at the total catastrophe and sight of the Earth's quake, burdens, and pulverized mountains; the believer asks in awe, while the unbeliever asks in astonishment.
rows.anchor: والأظهر هو الأول على أن المؤمن يقول ذلك بطريق الاستعظام والكافر بطريق التعجب

rows.speaker: غير واحد
rows.claim: More than one scholar takes the human here to mean the unbeliever who denies resurrection; the author prefers the broader sense including all people.
rows.anchor: وذهب غير واحد إلى أن المراد بالإنسان الكافر غير المؤمن بالبعث والأظهر هو الأول

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The phrase yawm idh may be an apposition to idha and adverb for the Earth speaking; the claim that the addressee is the subject, attributed to al-Tabarsi, has no basis. Other parses supply an implied verb, treat the time as an object of remembrance, or make it conditional with an implied answer.
rows.anchor: يومئذ بدل من إذا وقوله تعالى تحدث أخبارها أي الأرض واحتمال كون الفاعل المخاطب كما زعم الطبرسي لا وجه له

rows.speaker: ابن مسعود
rows.claim: Ibn Mas'ud and al-Thawri say God gives the Earth life and perception so it literally testifies to people's obedience and sins; a hasan sahih gharib report from Abu Hurayra through Ahmad and al-Tirmidhi says it testifies to each person's deeds on its surface, naming their day.
rows.anchor: وهو قول ابن مسعود والثوري وغيرهما ويشهد له الحديث الحسن الصحيح الغريب أخرج الإمام أحمد والترمذي عن أبي هريرة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The causal ba means the Earth speaks because its Lord instructed it; li is equivalent to ila, though revelation usually takes ila, and al-Ajjaj's verse attests li. The lām may instead mark purpose or benefit, since disclosure exposes wrongdoers.
rows.anchor: والباء في قوله تعالى بأن ربك أوحى لها للسببية أي تحدث بسبب إيحاء ربك لها وأمره سبحانه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The recipient may receive inspiration, or God may send an angel messenger to the Earth; if the Earth's speech is literal, revelation may create the life and power of speech.
rows.anchor: والوحي يحتمل أن يكون وحي إلهام وأن يكون وحي إرسال بأن يرسل سبحانه إليها رسولا من الملائكة

rows.speaker: الطبري
rows.claim: Al-Tabari and others treat the Earth's speech as metaphor: God creates signs in its condition that convey news in place of speech, enabling people to understand why it shook and expelled the dead.
rows.anchor: وقال الطبري وقوم التحديث استعارة أ

rows.speaker: يحيى بن سلام
rows.claim: Yahya ibn Sallam says the Earth reports what it has brought out; an Ibn Majah report has it say, Lord, this is what You entrusted to me.
rows.anchor: وقال يحيى بن سلام تحدث بما أخرجت من أثقالها ويشهد له ما في حديث ابن ماجه

rows.speaker: ابن مسعود
rows.claim: Ibn Mas'ud says the Earth announces that the Hour has begun when people ask what is wrong, answering that worldly life has ended and the afterlife has arrived.
rows.anchor: وعن ابن مسعود تحدث بقيام الساعة إذا قال الإنسان مالها فتخبر أن أمر الدنيا قد انقضى

rows.speaker: الزمخشري
rows.claim: Al-Zamakhshari proposes that the Earth's news is that its Lord revealed to it, treating the ba as emphatic; the author finds this interpretation remote.
rows.anchor: وقال الزمخشري يجوز أن يكون المعنى تحدث بتحديث أن ربك أوحى لها أخبارها

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Although the singular khabar would be expected, the plural أخبارها intensifies the meaning, as the cited example illustrates.
rows.anchor: وكان الظاهر تحدث بخبرها بالإفراد وكذا على ما قبله من الوجهين لكن جمع للمبالغة

rows.speaker: أبو حيان
rows.claim: Abu Hayyan harshly calls al-Zamakhshari's reading an indecency unfit for the Qur'an; al-Alusi says this rebuke is unjustified.
rows.anchor: وبالغ أبو حيان في الحط عليه فقال هو عفش ينزه القرآن عنه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: An alternative makes بأن ربك a substitute for أخبارها, since حدث can take direct or prepositional complements; despite grammatical defenses, this is far from the apparent sense, so the transmitted interpretation should be followed, especially if soundly reported.
rows.anchor: وجوز أيضا أن يكون بأن ربك الخ بدلا من أخبارها كأنه قيل يومئذ تحدث بأن ربك أوحى لها

rows.speaker: الزمخشري
rows.claim: Al-Zamakhshari and others, reportedly following Sibawayh, make حدث take two or three objects like verbs of cognition; أخبارها is the second, with the first omitted because who speaks is irrelevant.
rows.anchor: فذهب الزمخشري وغيره ونقل عن سيبويه إلى الثاني وهو عندهم ملحق بأفعال القلوب

rows.speaker: ابن الحاجب
rows.claim: Ibn al-Hajib argues that حدث takes one object and following words fill the place of an absolute object; al-Kashf objects that he conflates حديث and تحديث, since a ba-marked complement cannot be an absolute object. A defense says the source's effect may substitute for it.
rows.anchor: وقال الشيخ ابن الحاجب إنما هو متعد لواحد وما جاء بعده لتعين المفعول المطلق

rows.speaker: الطيبي
rows.claim: Al-Tibi says حدث and its cognates truly take one object; treating them as taking two or three is figurative or involves ellipsis of the sense of informing.
rows.anchor: وقال الطيبي يمكن أن يقال أن حدث وأخواتها متعديات إلى مفعول واحد حقيقة

rows.speaker: ابن مسعود
rows.claim: Ibn Mas'ud reads تنبئ أخبارها; Sa'id ibn Jubayr reads تنبئ with a light hamza.
rows.anchor: وقرأ ابن مسعود تنبيء أخبارها وسعيد بن جبير تنبيء بالتخفيف

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: People emerge from their graves to the reckoning in distinct groups and conditions: safe or fearful, riding or walking, chained or free; some early authorities say ranks from blessed to wretched, Ibn Abbas separates believers from unbelievers, and others understand individuals alone or people divided by regions.
rows.anchor: يخرجون من قبورهم بعد أن دفنوا فيها إلى موقف الحساب أشتاتا متفرقين بحسب طبقاتهم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Li-yuraw means that people may see the recompense of their deeds, either by eliding recompense or figuratively naming consequences as deeds; others say they see written records, actual embodied deeds, or learn the full details at judgment. The author rejects the embodied-deeds argument as unpersuasive.
rows.anchor: أي ليبصروا جزاء أعمالهم خيرا أو شرا فالرؤية بصرية والكلام على حذف مضاف

rows.speaker: النقاش
rows.claim: Al-Naqqash reads yasdur as departing after arriving at the gathering, with one group bound for Paradise and another Hell to see their recompense; the author finds this unconvincing.
rows.anchor: وقال النقاش الصدور مقابل الورود فيردون المحشر ويصدون منه متفرقين

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Li-yuraw is generally attached to yasdur; an alternative attaches it to awha with the intervening material parenthetical. Several authorities read liraw with an open yā.
rows.anchor: وقرأ الحسن والأعرج وقتادة وحماد بن سلمة والزهري وأبو حيوة وعيسى ونافع في رواية ليروا بفتح الياء

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The two clauses detail seeing deeds; dharra means a tiny, thin red ant, said to run after a year, or specks visible in sunlight, and is proverbial for the smallest measure. Imru al-Qays's verse illustrates the ant sense; Ibn Abbas demonstrated with dust.
rows.anchor: والذرة نملة صغيرة حمراء رقيقة ويقال أنها تجري إذا مضى لها حول وهي علم في القلة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Khayran and sharran are accusative as specification after an understood measure, or as substitutes for mithqal.
rows.anchor: وانتصاب خيرا وشرا على التمييز لأن مثقال ذرة مقدرا وقيل على البدلية من مثقال

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A general reading has every believer and unbeliever see the reward for even a speck of good or evil; this raises problems if unbelievers' good deeds are wholly voided and believers' minor sins forgiven when they avoid major sins.
rows.anchor: والظاهر أن من في الموضعين عامة للمؤمن والكافر وإن المراد من رؤية ما يعادل مثقال ذرة من خير أو شر

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: One solution reserves the first conditional for the fortunate and the second for the wretched; another keeps both general but supplies qualifications that good is seen if not voided and evil if not expiated.
rows.anchor: فالتزم بعضهم كون المراد بمن الأولى السعداء وبمن الثانية الأشقياء

rows.speaker: محمد بن كعب القرظي
rows.claim: Muhammad ibn Ka'b al-Qurazi says an unbeliever receives the worldly reward for good deeds, while a believer's evil is paid through worldly hardships, leaving no corresponding reward or punishment in the afterlife.
rows.anchor: فقد روي البغوي وابن جرير وابن المنذر وغيرهم عن محمد بن كعب القرظي

rows.speaker: أبو بكر
rows.claim: When Abu Bakr heard the verse, he asked about his speck of evil; the Prophet answered that disliked worldly events are recompense for specks of evil and good is stored until Resurrection. A version from Abu Ayyub says good is paid in the afterlife and evil through worldly illness and calamity.
rows.anchor: أخرج الطبراني في الأوسط البيهقي في الشعب وابن أبي حاتم وجماعة عن أنس قال بينما أبو بكر الصديق

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn Abbas says everyone, believer or unbeliever, is shown good and bad deeds: the believer's bad is forgiven and good rewarded, while the unbeliever's good is rejected and bad punished. The view that seeing means deeds themselves, leaving recompense to other evidence, preserves this distinction.
rows.anchor: عن ابن عباس من قوله في الآية ليس مؤمن ولا كافر عمل خيرا وشرا في الدنيا إلا أراه الله تعالى إياه

rows.speaker: الطيبي
rows.claim: Al-Tibi prefers the general reading: it matches the preceding promise that people emerge in different groups, comprehensively covers deeds and recompense, and fits the thoroughness of the weighing-of-deeds verse.
rows.anchor: واختار هذا الطيبي فقال إنه يساعده النظم والمعنى والأسلوب

rows.speaker: أبو هريرة
rows.claim: In the Bukhari-Muslim report about the charity owed on donkeys, the Prophet recites this comprehensive verse as his answer.
rows.anchor: روينا عن البخاري ومسلم عن أبي هريرة سئل صلى الله عليه وسلم عن الحمر

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The author prefers a general subject, seeing recompense, and an afterlife setting: the first clause is a promise that must occur by divine generosity, whereas the second is a threat whose outcome depends on revealed distinctions—disbelief is unforgiven, minor sins of the observant are expiated, and major or other sins remain under God's will.
rows.anchor: وأقول الظاهر عموم من وكون المراد رؤية الجزاء كما تقدم وكذا الظاهر كون ذلك في الآخرة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Sound reports of unbelievers' good deeds reducing punishment do not defeat the rule: disbelief's punishment is never reduced, while other degrees may be; works are voided insofar as they cannot save unbelievers from eternal punishment, not wholly, as al-Khafaji argues.
rows.anchor: ومعنى إحباط أعمال الكفار أنها لا تنجيهم من العذاب المخلد كأعمال غيرهم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Bukhari-Muslim report about the charity due on donkeys continues with the Prophet saying that no verse was revealed about it except this comprehensive, singular verse, which he recited.
rows.anchor: لم ينزل علي فيها شيء إلا هذه الآية الجامعة الفادة المتفردة في معناها

rows.speaker: صعصعة بن معاوية
rows.claim: Ahmad reports that Sa'sa'a ibn Mu'awiya, al-Farazdaq's uncle, heard the Prophet recite this verse and say it sufficed him, so he needed no other Qur'an.
rows.anchor: وروي الإمام أحمد عن صعصعة بن معاوية عم الفرزدق أنه أتى النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم فقرأ عليه الآية

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Some works on commentary say unbelievers receive worldly payment, not afterlife reward, for good deeds not requiring faith, such as rescuing the drowning or feeding a traveler; whether a later convert receives afterlife reward depends on when faith is required. Al-Karmani attributes mitigation to intercession, which may itself arise from the beneficiary's good.
rows.anchor: وما في التبصرة وشرح المشارق وتفسير الثعلبي من أن أعمال الكفرة الحسنة التي لا يشترط فيها الإيمان

rows.speaker: سعيد بن جبير
rows.claim: Ibn Abi Hatim reports Sa'id ibn Jubayr on the occasion of revelation: after 76:8, Muslims thought tiny charity earned no reward and minor sins incurred no threat; these verses urge even small good and warn against small evil.
rows.anchor: أخرج ابن أبي حاتم عن سعيد بن جبير أنه لما نزل ويطعمون الطعام على حبه كان المسلمون

rows.speaker: عائشة
rows.claim: Aisha divided a large donation from Ibn al-Zubayr among people while fasting, then had no money for meat to break her fast; she also gave a beggar one grape, saying it outweighed many specks. Similar examples are reported from Umar, Abd al-Rahman ibn Awf, and Sa'd ibn Malik to teach that small charity matters.
rows.anchor: فقد روي أن عائشة رض عنها بعث إليها ابن الزبير بمائة ألف وثمانين ألف درهم في غرارتين

rows.speaker: أنس بن مالك
rows.claim: Al-Zajjaji reports Anas's account of a beggar calling a date from the Prophet a prophet's donation; the Prophet says it contains many specks. Another report urges protection from Hell with half a date and recites the verse.
rows.anchor: أخرج الزجاجي في أماليه عن أنس بن مالك أن سائلا أتى النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم فأعطاه تمرة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Good is mentioned before evil because it is the nobler and primary concern; exhaustive accounting does not conflict with God's absolute generosity.
rows.anchor: وتقديم عمل الخير لأنه أشرف القسمين والمقصود بالأصالة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The segment introduces an anecdote in which a Bedouin reverses the order in the recitation and answers a correction with directions along either side of Harsha.
rows.anchor: وما يحكى من أن أعرابيا أخر خيرا يره فقيل له قدمت وأخرت فقال خذا بطن هرشي أو قفاها

rows.speaker: الحسين بن علي
rows.claim: The verse has variant readings of yirahu: a group reads the yā with ḍamma, while Hisham and Abu Bakr pause the final hā, Abu Amr lengthens it, and other canonical readers distinguish the two endings; Ikrima reads yarāhu with an alif, explained either by dialectal jussive form or a noncanonical relative reading.
rows.anchor: وقرأ الحسين ابن علي على جده وعليهما الصلاة والسلام وابن عباس رض عنهما وعبد الله بن مسلم وزيد بن علي

rows.speaker: ابن مسعود
rows.claim: The surah is Meccan according to Ibn Mas'ud, Jabir, al-Hasan, Ikrima, and Ata, and Medinan according to Anas, Qatada, and one transmission from Ibn Abbas; a report from Ibn Abbas says the Prophet sent cavalry and, after a month without news, the surah was revealed.
rows.anchor: مكية في قول ابن مسعود وجابر والحسن وعكرمة وعطاء مدنية في قول أنس وقتادة وإحدى الروايتين عن ابن عباس

rows.speaker: الحسن
rows.claim: A mursal report from al-Hasan and a marfu' report through Ata from Ibn Abbas say the surah equals half the Qur'an; the author has not found the reason for this merit.
rows.anchor: وأخرج أبو عبيد في فضائله من مرسل الحسن أنها تعدل بنصف القرآن

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The preceding surah describes reward for good and evil; this one censures those who prefer worldly life and fail to prepare with good deeds, with a link between the Earth's burdens released in 99:2 and the graves opened in 100:9.
rows.anchor: ولما ذكر سبحانه فيما قبلها الجزاء على الخير والشر أتبع ذلك فيها بتعنيت من آثر دنياه على آخرته

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The cavalry or camels move into an enemy gathering; the pronoun may refer to dust, with ba indicating accompaniment or causation. The fa-sequence orders the raid after running, sparks, and raising dust; several readers double the thā' or sīn with corresponding intensifying meanings.
rows.anchor: فوسطن به أي فتوسطن في ذلك الوقت جمعا من جموع الأعداء وجوز فيه وفي بائه نحو ما تقدم في به قبله

rows.speaker: ابن جني
rows.claim: Ibn Jinni says the doubled middle verb means the animals split the gathering into two halves; al-Zamakhshari instead treats the doubling as causative and the ba as emphasis, while an alternate derivation from thawwara is judged needless strain.
rows.anchor: وقال ابن جني المعنى ميزن به جمعا أي جعلنه شطرين أي قسمين وشقين

rows.speaker: علي
rows.claim: A report says Ali identifies the oath animals as pilgrims' camels: they run from Arafat to Muzdalifa, light fires there, then hurry at dawn to Mina; dust is raised by their feet. Ibn Abbas initially said war horses, then adopted Ali's answer after Ali noted only two horses were present at Badr.
rows.anchor: إنما العاديات ضبحا الإبل تعد من عرفة إلى المزدلفة فإذا أوو إلى المزدلفة أوروا النيران

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Badr objection does not establish that the verse refers to that battle: Ibn Abbas may mean horses generally, or a particular delayed expedition; the proposed defense based on Badr's special status is very weak. The report is likely unsound, al-Hakim is often too lenient, and transmissions conflict over Ali's interpretation; horses better raise dust, while the report implies both horses and camels plus warriors or pilgrims.
rows.anchor: والأحرى أن الخبر لا صحة له وتصحيح الحاكم محكوم عليه عند أهل الأثر بكثرة التساهل فيه

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Other interpretations distinguish the fire-makers from the oath animals: Ibn Abbas describes groups lighting fires for their needs or to frighten enemies, and Mujahid and Zayd ibn Aslam say they kindle a metaphorical fire by plotting in war. Ikrima's view that men's tongues ignite argument is called strange.
rows.anchor: ومن الغريب ما روي عن عكرمة أنها ألسنة الرجال توري النار من عظيم ما يتكلم به

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Esoteric readings make the charging creatures longing souls: their prayer sounds from yearning, thought kindles lights of knowledge, and they charge desire and habit toward sacred light, stirring longing to reach the ranks of the exalted.
rows.anchor: أن يكون المقسم به النفوس العادية أثر كما لهن الموريات بأفكارهن أنوار المعارف

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A second mystical interpretation maps the verse onto spiritual struggle: dhikr kindles guidance in the body, the soul crosses bodily darkness into the dawn of the self, stirs passing thoughts, then centers the heart's forces in the army of remembrance.
rows.anchor: الموريات بحوافر الذكر نار الهداية المستكنة فى حجر القالب وقت تخمير اللطيفة

rows.speaker: الحسن
rows.claim: Al-Hasan and Muhammad ibn Ka'b take the human as subject: his ingratitude is witnessed by its effects, a testimony of conduct more eloquent than speech; other readings make him testify aloud in the afterlife or knowingly commit ingratitude, heightening blame. The author favors the first.
rows.anchor: والظاهر الاول وقال ابن عباس وقتادة ضمير أنه عائد على الله تعالى

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn Abbas and Qatada instead refer the pronoun to God, who witnesses against the person as a warning; al-Tabrizi prefers this because the pronoun should return to the nearest antecedent. Al-Alusi says that rule is not compulsory and consistent pronouns favor the human.
rows.anchor: وقال ابن عباس وقتادة ضمير أنه عائد على الله تعالى أى وان ربه سبحانه شاهد عليه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-khayr means wealth in Qur'anic usage, sometimes abundant wealth; it is called good from people's perspective though wealth can become evil in the afterlife. The lām is causal: intense because of love of money.
rows.anchor: أى المال وورد بهذا المعنى فى القرآن هو المال وخصه بعضهم بالمال الكثير

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Shadid can mean miser, either passively tightened against generosity or actively keeping his money bag shut; more likely it means powerful, intensively loving wealth.
rows.anchor: وجوز غير واحد ان يراد بالشديد القوى ولعله الاظهر

rows.speaker: الزمخشري
rows.claim: Al-Zamakhshari reads him as strong in seeking money and worldly life but weak and slack in worship and gratitude to God; al-Alusi finds making the lām causal in that reading unclear.
rows.anchor: وهو لحب عبادة الله تعالى وشكر نعمته سبحانه ضعيف متقاعس

rows.speaker: الفراء
rows.claim: Al-Farra' explains the phrase as intense love of wealth, with the second occurrence of love omitted, like omitting wind after 'a stormy day'; Qutrub offers an alternative parsing as strong in love of wealth, which al-Alusi critiques as strained.
rows.anchor: وقال الفراء يجوز ان يكون المعنى وانه لحب الخير لشديد الحب يعنى انه يحب المال

rows.speaker: الزمخشري
rows.claim: Al-Zamakhshari's discussion also allows al-khayr to mean good deeds from God, with the human constricted and unresponsive toward them.
rows.anchor: ويفهم من كلام الزمخشرى فى الكشاف جواز أن يراد به ماهو عنده تعالى من الطاعات

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The interrogative is a threat: does the person not consider his fate when the dead are raised? The hamza denies, the fa connects to an implied premise, and the object of يعلم is omitted; idha is temporal. The author prefers this parsing.
rows.anchor: وأوجه الاوجه ماقدمناه وتعدى العلم اذا كان بمعنى المعرفة لواحد شائع

rows.speaker: الحوفي
rows.claim: Al-Hawfi makes idha govern يعلم, although the knowledge is in this life; a defense shifts the subject to God and treats knowing as punishment, but the author finds this forced. Other parses make idha an object of knowing or attach it to the raising, not to khabir after inna.
rows.anchor: وقال الحوفى العامل فى اذا الظرفية يعلم وأورد عليه أنه لايراد منه فى ذلك الوقت بل العلم فى الدنيا

rows.speaker: عبد الله
rows.claim: Abd Allah reads bu'thira with hā' and thā'; al-Aswad ibn Zayd reads baḥatha with those letters but no final rā'; Nasr ibn Asim has the first form in the active voice.
rows.anchor: وقرأ عبد الله بحثر بالحاء والثاء المثلثة وقرأ الاسود بن زيد بحث بهما بدون راء

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: What is in the hearts is gathered and exposed like a kernel from its husk, or sorted into good and evil; tahsil originally means extracting a core. Hearts are singled out because they originate bodily deeds and actions follow intentions, so the phrase explicitly and implicitly covers all deeds.
rows.anchor: وأصل التحصيل اخراج اللب من القشر كاخراج الذهب من حجر المعدن والبر من التبن

rows.speaker: ابن يعمر
rows.claim: Ibn Ya'mur and Nasr ibn Asim read ḥuṣṣila with the personified divine pronoun as agent; Ibn Ya'mur and Nasr also read ḥaṣṣala with a light ṣād, making what is gathered the subject.
rows.anchor: وقرأابن يعمر ونصر بن عاصم ومحمد بن أبي معدان وحصل مبنيا للفاعل وهو ضميره عز وجل

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Their Lord refers to the resurrected people, rationally described after their second life; He knows their very selves, qualities, and circumstances in detail on the day of the resurrection and heart-disclosure, with knowledge that entails recompense. Restricting the statement to that day signals the immediate judgment, not God's limited knowledge.
rows.anchor: أى عالم بظواهر ماعملوا وبواطنه علما موجبا للجزاء متصلا به كما ينىء عنه تقييده بذلك اليوم

rows.speaker: أبو السمال
rows.claim: Abu al-Simal and al-Hajjaj read inna with an open hamza and omit the emphatic lām; some take the clause as the object of يعلم, while another analysis supplies a causal lām linking it to the collection of hearts, which the author finds less apparent.
rows.anchor: وقرأ أبو السمال والحجاج ان ربهم بهم يومئذ خبير بفتح همزة أن واسقاط لام التاكيد

rows.speaker: الزمخشري
rows.claim: The day may be governed by an implied remember, by an implied impact of the Calamity (al-Zamakhshari), or by an implied occurrence; some place the verb earlier, while Ibn Atiyya attaches it directly to al-qari'a. Abu Hayyan objects to the latter parses on syntactic and semantic grounds; Zayd ibn Ali's nominative reading supports it.
rows.anchor: وقال الزمخشري ظرف لمضمر دلت عليه القارعة أي تقرع يوم

rows.speaker: قتادة
rows.claim: Al-Farash is commonly read, following Qatada, as moths that fly and plunge into fire; others describe fine birds repeatedly hitting the lamp, while al-Farra' says it is a swarm of locusts climbing over one another. The views all suggest confusion and agitation, but many prefer Qatada's image of people scattered, weak, humiliated, disorderly, and moving toward the caller from every direction; Jarir's verse illustrates the comparison.
rows.anchor: واختار غير واحد ماروى عن قتادة وقالوا شبهوا في الكثرة والانتشار والضعف والذلة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The mountains become wool, either wool generally or dyed wool as al-Raghib specifies; manfush means pulled apart by fingers so the fragments scatter and fly through the air, as other verses describe.
rows.anchor: أي الصوف مطلقا أو المصبوغ كما قيده الراغب به

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The question followed by blazing fire explains the previously obscure Hawiya and signals its unfamiliar, terrifying scale; the name may describe an extreme depth, with a report saying the people of Hell fall for seventy years, or identify its lowest gate. Calling the abode a mother suggests refuge or enclosing shelter, perhaps mockingly.
rows.anchor: فانه تقرير لها بعد ابهامها والاشعار بخروجها عن المعهود للتفخيم والتهويل

rows.speaker: قتادة
rows.claim: Qatada, Abu Salih, Ikrima, al-Kalbi, and others say the sinner's head falls into Hell's depths; another Qatada report takes the expression as an Arabic imprecation for death and a mother's grief. Ka'b ibn Sa'd's verse witnesses the latter; al-Kashf prefers it for its parallel with a pleasing life, and al-Tibi calls it more apparent, though al-Alusi leaves room for debate.
rows.anchor: وعن قتادة وأبي صالح وعكرمة والكلبي وغيرهم المعنى فام رأسه هاوية في قعر جهنم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: In the second reading, the pronoun refers to the catastrophe implied by the discourse; alternatively it refers to Hawiya or what the discourse suggests. The hā' in hiyah is a pause marker, omitted in connected recitation by Ibn Abi Ishaq, al-A'mash, and Hamza but retained by most.
rows.anchor: والضمير أعنى هي عليه للداهية التي التي دل عليها الكلام وعلى ما قدمناه لهاوية

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Nār is the predicate of an omitted subject and ḥāmiyah qualifies it, from intense heat; the derivation meaning merely 'possessing heat' is unconvincing. Talha reads fa-ummuhu with kasra, reported by Ibn Khalawayh and Ibn Durayd as a dialect, although grammarians allow kasra only after a preceding kasra or yā'.
rows.anchor: ورفع نار على انها خبر مبتدأ محذوف أي هي نار وحامية نعت لها وهو من الحمى اشتداد الحر

rows.speaker: أبو بريدة
rows.claim: Although many call the surah Meccan, al-Alusi chooses Medina based on Abu Burayda's report: two Ansari clans boast of living ancestors, then go to the graves to boast of the dead, prompting its revelation. A report from Ubayy says the warning about Adam's desire for a third valley continued until the surah descended; Ali says it ended doubts about grave punishment, which al-Alusi takes as Medinan evidence because that punishment is mentioned in a Medinan context.
rows.anchor: عن أبي بريدة فيها قال نزلت في قبيلتين من قبائل الانصار في بني حارثة وبني الحرث تفاخروا وتكاثروا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The surah has eight verses unanimously; reports also call it equal to a thousand verses, and its connection with the preceding surah is evident.
rows.anchor: وآيها ثمان بالاتفاق وهي تعدل ألف آية من القرآن

rows.speaker: ناصر الدين بن الميلق
rows.claim: Ibn al-Milq explains the thousand-verse merit as one sixth of the Qur'an's roughly 6,200 verses: al-Ghazali's six aims include knowledge of the return to God, which this surah contains. Al-Alusi says the matter lies beyond this calculation.
rows.anchor: ذكر ناصر الدين بن الميلق في سر ذلك أن القرآن ستة آلاف ومائتا آية وكسر

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Kalla rebukes preoccupation with what does not matter and warns that its outcome is grave; soon the hearers will recognize the evil consequence when they witness it.
rows.anchor: ردع عن الاشتغال بما لايعنيه عما يعنيه وتنبه على الخطأ فيه لان عاقبته وخيمة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Repeating the warning reinforces it, while thumma makes the second more emphatic, like a master repeating a command; some say the second is treated as different to allow coordination. Though grammarians reportedly disallow coordinating an emphatic clause, commentators and grammarians explicitly allow it.
rows.anchor: تكرير للتأكيد وثم للدلالة على أن الثاني أبلغ كما يقول العظيم لعبده أقول لك ثم أقول لك

rows.speaker: علي بن أبي طالب
rows.claim: Ali says the first warning applies in the graves and the second at resurrection, so the clauses are not repetitive and thumma is temporal; al-Dahhak instead assigns the first to unbelievers and the later to believers, contrary to the apparent sense.
rows.anchor: وقال علي ابن أبي طالب كرم الله تعالى وجهه الاول في القبور والثاني في النشور

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Knowledge with certainty means knowing what lies ahead with the certainty one has about established matters; the genitive may mean knowledge of what is certain, or, with Abu Hayyan, certain knowledge contrasted with less certain knowledge. The omitted result of law intensifies the warning: they would act immeasurably or be distracted from boasting.
rows.anchor: أى لو تعلمون مابين أيديكم علم الأمر المتيقن أي كعلمكم ماتستيقنونه من الامور

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: La-tarawunna is the answer to an unstated oath, strengthening the threat and clarifying the fate after deliberate ambiguity; it cannot answer the counterfactual law because the vision is certain to occur.
rows.anchor: جواب قسم مضمور أكد به الوعيد وشدد به التهديد وأوضح به ماأنذروه بعد ابهامه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Some make it the answer to law, meaning they will know their fate and then continuously see Hell; the author rejects this as far-fetched because Hell would never leave their sight.
rows.anchor: وقيل يجوز ويكون المعنى سوف تعلمون الجزاء ثم قال سبحانه لو تعلمون الجزاء علم اليقين
